Awake again. This is the fourth night this week. Writing so I stop pretending.

The next morning they rode there together. Sitting on the bench outside the doctor's room, Abhinav felt ashamed. Wasim nudged him. 'Asking takes more guts than chewing, yaar.' Abhinav went in.

passage:
Hi Amandeep,
You asked why I've been so much less grumpy lately. Honestly? I stopped doomscrolling.
For months I'd get into bed and read news, then everyone's highlights, then more news. I'd feel tense, jealous, sure the world was ending and my life was behind everyone's. And then I'd lie awake till two.
Three weeks ago I tried a wind-down time. At ten-thirty the phone goes on charge in the kitchen. I make tea, read a paper book, and lights off by eleven-thirty. The first few nights I felt twitchy without it. Now I sleep better and wake up less heavy. Nothing dramatic. Just quieter.
Try it with me?
Gargi

qa.a: In the kitchen.

qa.a: Gargi felt tense and jealous, sure life was falling behind everyone else's.

subtype: Working screens late into the night [Actor]
passage: When I started at the design studio, my manager Damini sent messages at midnight, and I answered every one within minutes. I thought that was what being good at the job looked like. I'm Vandana, and for about six months I went to bed with my phone buzzing on the pillow. Even when it was quiet, my mind kept buzzing, rehearsing replies. I woke up every morning feeling I hadn't slept at all. One evening I asked Damini, nervously, whether she expected instant replies at night. She looked surprised. 'No! I just send them when I think of them.' After that I turned notifications off at nine and put the phone in the other room at ten-thirty. The first week felt wrong. Now I sleep through, and my work is actually better.

qa.q: When did Damini send messages?
qa.a: At midnight.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel in the mornings during those six months?
qa.a: Vandana felt unrested and drained, as if there had been no sleep at all.

qa.q: Which choice made the biggest difference?
qa.a: Asking Damini about expectations, then turning notifications off at nine and moving the phone to another room at ten-thirty.

qa.q: How might Damini have felt learning Vandana replied at midnight?
qa.a: Damini was surprised and probably a little concerned, not having meant to pressure anyone.

grounding: Shows a professional replying to messages late at night whose mind keeps buzzing, and who sets work boundaries and a screen-free time before sleep.

I've noticed Aadhya replying to client emails at 1 am, sometimes later. In meetings she looks pale, loses track of points and admitted she 'can't switch off' even when she stops working. Devika

passage:
Monday: At her new school, Shalini, nine, walked in with her shoulders hunched and her eyes on her shoes. At home she curled up small on the sofa and said, 'Nobody talks to me.'
Saturday: Urmila Maasi came to visit. 'Let's play Tall Tree!' They stretched their arms up to the ceiling, stood on tiptoe, swayed like trees in a storm and roared like lions. Shalini giggled. 'Stand like a tree and see how you feel.' Shalini stood tall. 'A bit bigger.'
The next Monday: Before assembly, Shalini remembered the tree. She lifted her chin and stood tall. She still felt shy, but when a girl in her line said hi, Shalini looked up and said hi back.

qa.q: What game did Urmila Maasi play with Shalini?
qa.a: Tall Tree.

qa.q: How was Shalini feeling on the first Monday?
qa.a: She felt lonely and small, hunching and looking at her shoes.

qa.q: What did Urmila Maasi do that helped?
qa.a: She made stretching and standing tall into a playful game, which lifted Shalini a little.

qa.q: How might the girl in the line have seen Shalini?
qa.a: She probably saw a new girl who looked up and seemed friendly enough to talk to.

grounding: Shows a shy, sad child hunching and looking down, and playful stretching and standing tall lifting her a little.

passage: Raghav, come, sit up straight for your Naveen Dada, eh? I know that slump. When I was your age, ten, in our town near Mangaluru, I was the smallest and shyest boy in class. I walked hunched over, looking at my sandals. The more I hunched, the smaller I felt. Then our PE teacher, a big laughing man named Mr D'Costa, started a game every morning. 'Everybody, be a giraffe!' We had to stretch our necks, walk on tiptoe, reach for invisible leaves. I felt silly. But one day, after being a giraffe, I noticed I was standing tall at the blackboard, and my voice came out louder. Your Dadi says I still walk like a giraffe. Now, let's see you be one.

qa.q: What was Naveen's PE teacher called?
qa.a: Mr D'Costa.

qa.q: How did young Naveen feel walking hunched over?
qa.a: Young Naveen felt shy and small, and the more he hunched, the smaller he felt.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Naveen's story?
qa.a: Playing the giraffe game every morning, which one day left Naveen standing tall and speaking louder at the blackboard.

qa.q: How might Mr D'Costa have seen the shy boys in his class?
qa.a: He probably noticed their hunched shoulders and used a silly game to help them lift up without singling anyone out.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a shy child whose hunching made him feel smaller, and how playful stretching and standing tall lifted his energy.

passage: Payal's best friend had moved to Chennai, and for a week Payal, ten, had barely lifted her head. That Sunday it poured, the power went out in the afternoon, and her aunt Jyoti found her slumped on the floor, chin on her knees. There was no TV, no phone charge, nothing to do. 'Right,' said Jyoti. 'Candle-light disco.' She sang loudly and badly. 'Arms up! Stretch! Now star jumps!' Payal rolled her eyes. Then, slowly, she stood up and stretched. Jyoti made her do a superhero pose, hands on hips, chin up. 'How does that feel?' Payal thought. 'Still sad. But a bit less small.' They danced by candlelight until the lights came back, and Payal laughed for the first time that week.

qa.q: Where had Payal's best friend moved?
qa.a: To Chennai.

qa.q: How was Payal feeling that Sunday?
qa.a: She was sad and missing her friend, slumped with her chin on her knees.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do that helped a little?
qa.a: She turned the power cut into a playful disco with stretches, star jumps and a superhero pose.

qa.q: How might Jyoti have felt seeing Payal laugh?
qa.a: She was probably relieved and happy to see her niece laugh after a sad week.

grounding: Shows a sad child slumped and feeling small, and playful movement, stretching and standing tall lifting her energy a little.
